The coaches would also like to thank former academic director, Dr. Larry Kirkpatrick for his many helpful comments.

problems.statement: A tennis ball launcher is placed on the floor at the front end of a train that has a uniform forward acceleration of $2.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. The launcher projects a ball at an initial speed of $25.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ with respect to the train toward its rear. The ball achieves a maximum height of $10.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Ignore air resistance.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find $\theta_o$, the angle of launch with respect to the floor.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find how far from the front end of the train the ball lands.

answer.note: The ball lands 67.3 m behind the front end (official: Δx = −67.3 m; either sign okay, 67.4 m also okay).

solution.statement:
1. $y_{\max} = 10\ \mathrm{m}$ $\quad v_o = 25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ $\quad a = 2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

a. The train's acceleration does not affect the vertical motion.

At the highest point, $v_y = 0$ **[2]**

$v_y^2 = v_{oy}^2 - 2gy$ **[2]**

$v_{oy} = \sqrt{2gy_{\max}} = \sqrt{2(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})(10\ \mathrm{m})} = 14\ \mathrm{m/s}$ **[2]**

Since $v_{oy} = v_o \sin\theta$ **[2]**

$\theta = \sin^{-1}\left(v_{oy}/v_o\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(14\ \mathrm{m/s} / 25\ \mathrm{m/s}\right) = 34.1^{\circ}$ **[2]**

b. The time to reach $y_{\max}$ is obtained from $v_y = v_{oy} - gt$ at the highest point

$t = \dfrac{v_{oy}}{g} = \dfrac{14\ \mathrm{m/s}}{9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}} = 1.43\ \mathrm{s}$ **[5]**

The time to land is twice that, or $t = 2.86$ s. **[2]**

During that time, the ball moves a distance $x_b = v_{oc}t - v_o\cos\theta t$ **[2]**

where $v_{oc}$ is the velocity of the train with respect to the Earth when the ball is launched.

And the front end of the train moves $x_p = v_{oc}t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ **[2]**

The difference of those displacements is the ball's displacement with respect to the train.

$\Delta x = x_b - x_p = -v_o\cos\theta t - \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ **[2]**

$\Delta x = -25\ \mathrm{m/s}\left(\cos 34.1^{\circ}\right)2.86\ \mathrm{s} - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\right)\left(2.86\ \mathrm{s}\right)^2 = -67.3\ \mathrm{m}$ **[2]**

(Either sign okay. 67.4 m also okay. Part b may also be solved in the train's accelerating frame or in an inertial frame with the same velocity with respect to the Earth that the train had when the ball was launched. Any correct method may be used.)

problems.statement: A cube of mass M starts at rest at point A at a height of 4R, where R is the radius of the circular part of the track. The cube slides down the track and around the loop. The cube is very small compared to the size of the track.

figures.alt: Track diagram: a small square cube at point A at the top of a vertical track that curves down and into a circular loop of radius R; point B (with a small square) is at the top of the loop. A grey double-headed vertical arrow labelled 4R marks the height of A, and a grey horizontal arrow labelled R marks the loop radius.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Assuming the track is frictionless, find the force the track exerts on the cube at point B. Express your answer as a function of Mg.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: The cube is replaced by a sphere with mass M and radius r ($r \ll R$). Assuming that the sphere starts at the same height 4R and rolls without slipping, find the force the track exerts on the sphere at point B. Express your answer as a function of Mg.

solution.statement:
2. a. Apply energy conservation to equate total energy at point A and point B. **[2]**

$4MgR = 2MgR + \tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2$ **[3]**

$Mv^2 = 4MgR$ **[1]**

Applying Newton's 2$^{\mathrm{nd}}$ law to the forces at point B **[2]**

$N + Mg = M\dfrac{v^2}{R}$ **[4]**

$N + Mg = \dfrac{(4MgR)}{R}$ **[1]**

or $N = 3Mg$ downward **[2]**

b. Since it is rolling at point B, it also has rotational kinetic energy there

$4MgR = 2MgR + \tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\omega^2$ **[3]**

With $\omega = v/R$ **[3]**

$2MgR = \left(\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{2}{5}\right)Mv^2 = \tfrac{7}{10}Mv^2$ **[1]**

$N + Mg = \dfrac{\left(\tfrac{20}{7}MgR\right)}{R}$ **[1]**

Thus $N = \tfrac{13}{7}Mg$ downward **[2]**

problems.statement: Two masses, $m_1$ and $m_2$, attached to equal length massless strings, are hanging side-by-side just in contact with each other. Mass $m_1$ is swung out to the side to a point having a vertical displacement $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ above mass $m_2$. It is then released from rest and collides elastically with the stationary hanging mass $m_2$. Each of the masses is observed to rise to the same height following the collision.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the numerical value of this height.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: The masses swing back down and undergo a second elastic collision. Describe what happens following the second collision. (A proof is not required.)

answer.value: After the second collision m₂ stops and m₁ reaches the maximum height hᵢ = 0.20 m.

solution.statement:
3. Let $h_i = 0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ the initial height of $m_1$.

$h_f$ = the final height of both masses.

$v_{1i}$ = the speed of $m_1$ just before the collision.

$v_{1f}$ = the speed of $m_1$ just after the collision.

$v_{2f}$ = the speed of $m_2$ just after the collision.

a. Before the collision, for $m_1$ $\quad m_1gh_i = \tfrac{1}{2}m_1v_{1i}^2$ **[3]**

After the collision, for $m_1$ $\quad m_1gh_f = \tfrac{1}{2}m_1v_{1f}^2$

After the collision, for $m_2$ $\quad m_2gh_f = \tfrac{1}{2}m_2v_{2f}^2$

Since both masses rise to the same height after the collision, they must have equal speeds after the collision $\quad v_{1f} = v_{2f} = v_f$ **[3]**

Since the collision is elastic, the total kinetic energy is unchanged **[2]**

$\tfrac{1}{2}m_1v_{1i}^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}m_1v_f^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m_2v_f^2$ **[2]**

or $\quad m_1gh_i = m_1gh_f + m_2gh_f$

$m_1h_i = (m_1 + m_2)h_f \qquad \text{Eq. 1}$ **[2]**

Using momentum conservation **[2]**

$m_1v_{1i} = m_2v_f - m_1v_f$ **[2]**

or $\quad m_1\sqrt{2gh_i} = (m_2 - m_1)\sqrt{2gh_f}$

$m_1\sqrt{h_i} = (m_2 - m_1)\sqrt{h_f}$

Squaring both sides $\quad m_1^2h_i = \left(m_2^2 - 2m_1m_2 + m_1^2\right)h_f$

Substituting in Eq. 1 $\quad m_1(m_1 + m_2)h_f = \left(m_2^2 - 2m_1m_2 + m_1^2\right)h_f$

Solving for the relation between the masses $\quad 0 = m_2^2 - 3m_2m_1$

Or assuming $m_2 \neq 0$ $\quad m_2 = 3m_1$ **[2]**

Solving Eq. 1 for $h_f$ $\quad h_f = \dfrac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2}h_i = \dfrac{m_1}{m_1 + 3m_1}h_i = \dfrac{1}{4}0.20\ \mathrm{m} = 0.050\ \mathrm{m}$ **[2]**

b. After the second collision $m_2$ stops **[3]**

and $m_1$ reaches maximum height $h_i$ **[2]**

problems.statement:
A car accelerates uniformly from rest. Initially, its door is slightly ajar. Calculate how far the car travels before the door slams shut. Assume the door has a frictionless hinge, a uniform mass distribution, and a length L from front to back.

(contributed by Leaf Turner)

solution.statement:
4. Imagine the door to be a compound pendululm in a gravitational field whose “g” equals the car's acceleration. We are interested in finding 1/4 of the period of the oscillation, the time it takes the door to go from a maximum small amplitude to its equilibrium position. The torque and rotational inertia are:

Diagram similar to accompanying **[5]**

$\tau = -Ma\left(L/2\right)\sin\theta$ **[3]**

$I = \left(1/3\right)ML^2$ **[4]**

$\left(1/3\right)ML^2\alpha = -Ma\left(L/2\right)\sin\theta$ **[3]**

For small angles we have $\quad \alpha \equiv -\left(3/2\right)\left(a/L\right)\theta$ **[1]**

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{3a}{2L}$ **[3]**

$t = \dfrac{T}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{3a}}$ **[2]**

The distance the car travels is $\quad D = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}a\dfrac{\pi^2}{4}\left(\dfrac{2L}{3a}\right) = \dfrac{\pi^2}{12}L$ **[4]**

figures.alt: Door drawn as a long thin rectangle of length L, tilted from its hinge (dot at the top) by the angle θ from the vertical dashed direction; a force arrow Ma points down from the middle of the door; the lever arm is labelled (L/2)sinθ.
